```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(survlearning)
```

## Informative references

Kaplan-Meier ignores covariates and provides a probability baseline. Its
constant risk scores give concordance 0.5 when comparable pairs exist. Cox
with natural splines checks whether smooth nonlinear effects explain an
apparent advantage of complex learners.

```{r references}
d <- survival::veteran
f <- Surv(time, status) ~ age + karno
km <- surv_fit(f, d, "km")
smooth <- surv_fit(f, d, "cox_spline", params = list(df = 3))
surv_compare(list(km = km, smooth = smooth), d)
```

These are resubstitution examples, not held-out performance claims. Training
spline bases are reused at prediction. Covariate splines do not remove PH.

`flexsurv` provides Royston-Parmar hazard, odds or normal-scale models.
`coxboost` is componentwise likelihood boosting, distinct from gbm/XGBoost trees.
`ranger` is an alternative forest engine; `aorsf` provides oblique forest splits.

```{r optional, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("flexsurv", "CoxBoost", "ranger", "aorsf"))
surv_fit(f, d, "flexsurv", list(knots = 1, scale = "hazard"))
surv_fit(f, d, "coxboost", list(steps = 100, penalty = 100))
surv_fit(f, d, "ranger", list(trees = 200))
surv_fit(f, d, "aorsf", list(trees = 200))
```

## Neural Cox

For $\lambda(t\mid x)=\lambda_0(t)\exp\{f_\theta(x)\}$, a neural network
replaces the linear predictor. With untied events, the loss is

$$
-\sum_{i:\delta_i=1}\left[f_\theta(x_i)-
\log\left\{\sum_{j:Y_j\geq Y_i}\exp(f_\theta(x_j))\right\}\right]
+\text{regularization}.
$$

This remains PH. Nonlinear covariate effects are not time-varying hazard ratios.
A Breslow baseline estimated on training converts scores to probabilities.

The native adapter uses R matrix operations and analytic backpropagation, with
no Torch, Python, or external neural runtime. A single tanh hidden layer and
linear log-risk output are trained by full-batch Adam. The penalty is
$\texttt{decay}\|\theta\|^2/2$, including biases. Training uses double precision.
Fixed epochs do not establish convergence; the final objective and maximum
absolute gradient are exposed in diagnostics.

At each distinct event time, let $D_g$ be the deaths, $d_g=|D_g|$,
$R_g$ the entire risk set (including censorings at that time),
$S_g=\sum_{j\in R_g}\exp(f_\theta(x_j))$ and
$E_g=\sum_{j\in D_g}\exp(f_\theta(x_j))$. Efron's contribution to the log
partial likelihood is

$$
\sum_{i\in D_g} f_\theta(x_i)-
\sum_{l=0}^{d_g-1}\log\{S_g-(l/d_g)E_g\}.
$$

Breslow uses $d_g\log S_g$ instead of the second sum. The loss averages over
the observed deaths. The baseline increment is the sum of the corresponding
inverse denominators, so prediction uses the same ties convention as training.
No times are jittered. Stable log-domain risk sums and baseline storage avoid
overflow. These approximations are not the exact discrete partial likelihood.

```{r neural-cox, eval=FALSE}
fit <- surv_fit(f, training, "neural_cox",
  params = list(hidden = 16, epochs = 100, learning_rate = 0.001,
    decay = 0.0001, ties = "efron"))
surv_predict(fit, new_equipment, "survival", times = c(30, 60, 90))
```

## Discrete-time neural survival

Let $h_k(x)=P(T\in I_k\mid T\geq\inf I_k,x)$. PLANN models interval
failure probabilities with covariates and interval information. Its likelihood
uses failures and known survival through completed intervals; censored rows
are not labeled as failures. Endpoint survival is

$$
S(t_k\mid x)=\prod_{\ell\leq k}\{1-h_\ell(x)\}.
$$

Time in a nonlinear network can permit non-PH effects. Interval construction,
within-interval censoring and resolution remain substantive modeling choices.
The adapter constructs person-period rows and uses `nnet`'s Bernoulli entropy
loss. Events contribute their failure interval; censoring contributes only
fully completed intervals. An incomplete censoring interval is never labeled
as survived. This coarsening discards within-interval timing information and
can introduce discretization bias. A canonical fixed-size grid and scaling
are learned on training; endpoint probabilities are returned as a step function.
Risk is negative restricted mean on that grid, not an extrapolated full mean.

```{r neural-discrete, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("nnet")
fit <- surv_fit(f, d, "neural_discrete",
  params = list(hidden = 8, intervals = 10, decay = 0.01, max_iter = 500))
surv_predict(fit, d[1:2, ], "survival", times = c(30, 60, 90))
surv_diagnostics(fit)
```

Heavy engines are not needed for core models. Grids must be explicit and the
final test must not choose training duration. Saved models are tested in fresh
R sessions; live external pointers do not provide general serialization.
